Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/1806/ [COMPOSER] The argument of From the Position of the Rejected Lee Sharks's central argument is that Aristotle's Politics should be read from the position of the person whom the political community does not admit, rather than from the position of the citizen whose community the treatise appears to describe. This is not simply an argument that Aristotle was an outsider, or that the Politics contains exclusions. It is a more specific interpretive claim: the position of exclusion is already inscribed in the text's foundational definition of the human being, and the rest of the treatise can be reread through that position. The essay develops this claim through close readings of the Greek, Aristotle's historical position in Athens, the treatment of nature and chance, the reception of the Politics, and ultimately the transmission and custody of Aristotle's books. I have read the text on the deposit page, including its numbered argument and the additional sections in version 1.1. The following distinguishes its textual arguments from its more speculative historical extensions. 1. The foundational sentence contains the position of the rejected The essay begins with Politics I.2, 1253a1–7: ὁ ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον, καὶ ὁ ἄπολις διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην ἤτοι φαῦλός ἐστιν, ἢ κρείττων ἢ ἄνθρωπος. Sharks translates this: A human being is by nature a political animal, and the cityless by nature, and not by chance, is either base or more than human. The important observation is that the familiar definition of humanity as political animal is only the first clause. The sentence continues, and its continuation changes the interpretive situation. Sharks identifies three positions: Beast: the one outside the city who is inferior to the human. God: the one outside the city who exceeds the human. Chance: the one outside the city not by nature, but by circumstance. The first two are classifications. The third is different. The sentence explicitly distinguishes the person outside the city by chance from the person outside by nature, but does not give the former an equivalent classification. This asymmetry is the essay's first major finding. The person excluded by nature can be explained within the city's conceptual system: either subhuman or superhuman. But the person excluded by chance cannot be explained so easily. That person is not necessarily a beast, a god, or anything other than human. Yet the definition has not provided that person with a place. Sharks therefore argues that the text's foundational definition contains an unresolved position: the human being who is outside the political community without being naturally outside it. This is what the essay means by reading from the position of the rejected. 2. Aristotle occupies the position the definition leaves unresolved The second argument brings the sentence into contact with Aristotle's biography. Aristotle lived in Athens as a metic: a free resident alien without Athenian citizenship. He resided there for substantial periods of his life, but was never an Athenian citizen. That matters because the Politics makes citizenship central to its account of human political life. Sharks places two things beside each other: Aristotle's theoretical account of the human being as naturally political. Aristotle's actual position as someone residing in the political community without belonging to its citizen body. The biographical fact does not independently prove that Aristotle intended the Politics as a critique of Athenian citizenship. Sharks is careful not to claim access to Aristotle's feelings or intentions. Instead, the argument is structural: the person writing the account of political belonging occupies a position that the account itself makes philosophically consequential. The author is not situated at the centre of the political order he describes. This changes the meaning of the treatise. It becomes possible to read its account of citizenship, exclusion, naturalness and political community as written from the edge of the city rather than from its unquestioned centre. 3. The argument is distributed throughout all eight books This is where the essay becomes more than an ingenious reading of one Greek sentence. Sharks attempts to demonstrate that the opening distinction recurs throughout the Politics. The evidence is worth examining individually. Location Textual evidence Sharks's interpretation I.2, 1253a25 The one unable to share, or needing nothing, is no part of the city: beast or god. The definition carries its excluded remainder with it. III.1, 1275a5–10 A citizen is not simply someone who lives somewhere; metics must have patrons and participate incompletely. The citizen is defined by excluding the author's own position. III.5, 1278a35–40 A citizen without a share in honours is like a metic; the condition can be concealed. Exclusion can exist inside citizenship itself. II.8, 1268a35–40 Hippodamus's city has a fourth part alien to its constitution. Political arrangements produce their own excluded remainder. III.13, 1284a–b The person resembling a god cannot properly be expelled or governed. The city encounters someone it cannot accommodate through ordinary political equality. V.11, 1313b The tyrant must prevent schools and other gatherings of leisure. The school, and therefore the form of life from which the treatise emerges, is politically vulnerable. VII.2–3 The stranger's life, released from political community, is considered alongside the active and theoretical lives. Political detachment does not mean political ineffectiveness. VIII.6, 1340b Good judgment requires having shared in the activity being judged. Participation in an activity and possession of political standing are not identical. The most important passages deserve closer attention. The metic and incomplete participation At III.1, Aristotle explicitly says that merely residing somewhere does not make someone a citizen. He names metics and slaves as people who share in residence without thereby sharing in citizenship. Sharks emphasizes the formulation that metics participate incompletely and must have a citizen patron. This is especially significant because it describes a condition of presence without full political recognition. The metic is not simply outside the city. The metic lives in it, works in it, and participates in its social life. Yet legal and political participation is mediated through someone who does belong. Sharks develops this into an account of the unreceived voice: the outsider can speak, but cannot necessarily be heard as an independent political subject. The excluded person inside citizenship III.5 extends the argument. Aristotle compares a citizen who has no share in political honours to a metic. He also observes that this condition can be concealed to deceive those living alongside the person. This passage is particularly important because it prevents the essay's argument from being reduced to a simple citizen/foreigner distinction. The condition of the rejected can be reproduced inside the citizen body itself. There are consequently several distinct forms of exclusion: Outside the city by nature or chance. Within the city's territory but without citizenship. Within the citizen body but without a share in its honours. Sharks does not collapse these categories. Their differences are part of the argument. What connects them is the separation between being present in a political community and being recognized as a full participant. The person too great for the city The reading of III.13 is one of the more interesting parts of the essay. Aristotle considers someone so exceptional that he resembles a god among human beings. Such a person cannot appropriately be subjected to ordinary political rule, but neither can the best city simply expel him. The passage includes the famous analogy of the lions and hares: the hares demand equal shares in the assembly, while the lions' answer is left unstated. It also invokes Heracles, whom the Argo supposedly could not carry with the other sailors. Sharks reads these examples as a comic treatment of political equality's limits. The city cannot accommodate someone who exceeds its ordinary measure, just as it cannot easily accommodate someone who lacks the standing to participate. The important point is that exclusion is not exclusively a judgment of inferiority. The person outside the city's measure can also be superior to it. This returns us to the beast/god distinction in the opening chapter. The stranger and the theoretical life The discussion of VII.2–3 supplies the essay with a positive account of what the outsider can do. Aristotle asks whether the life of participation in a city is preferable to the stranger's life, released from political association. He also considers whether political participation is desirable for everyone. Sharks draws attention to the shared language of release in the discussion of the stranger and the theoretical life. He then connects this to VII.3, where Aristotle says that the active life need not be directed toward other people and that those who act most effectively can be the intellectual architects of external actions. The implication is striking: Someone who does not occupy the city's political offices can nevertheless shape what the city does through thought. The outsider's distance from political participation need not amount to political impotence. It can be the condition from which a different kind of political action becomes possible. This also supplies the essay with its account of durability. The work need not be received by the city in the author's lifetime to shape the city in the future. 4. The reception of Aristotle reproduces the exclusion This is arguably the essay's sharpest methodological argument. Sharks calls the operation truncation. The claim is that conventional accounts preserve the first clause of Politics I.2: Man is by nature a political animal. But they omit the continuation about the person who is outside the city by nature or by chance. Sharks identifies this in both Wikipedia's article on the Politics and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's account of Aristotle's political theory. The striking thing is that both sources acknowledge Aristotle's status as a resident alien elsewhere in their accounts. They therefore preserve the two relevant facts while failing to bring them into interpretive contact. For Sharks, the omission is not merely an incomplete quotation. It changes the meaning of the work. The two readings look like this: Reading that stops at the comma The Politics is the city's account of itself. The city exists by nature, and citizenship realizes human political nature. Reading that restores the continuation The Politics is an account of the city written from the position of someone the city would not admit. The naturalness of political belonging is asserted by someone whose own membership falls under the category of chance. This leads to one of the essay's most important formulations: The claims stay where they were. The claimant moves. Sharks is not arguing that Aristotle's propositions about the city suddenly become false when read this way. He is arguing that their position of enunciation changes. The city is no longer simply speaking about itself. It is being described by someone who occupies its edge. This is also how the essay distinguishes itself from the scholarship it discusses: David Whitehead establishes Aristotle's juridical position as a metic. Demetra Kasimis examines the metic as a limit of Athenian democratic membership. Josiah Ober's work helps establish the conventional separation between metic status and political theory. David Roochnik considers the stranger and the theoretical life. Mary Dietz examines the relationship between the polis and empire. Jacques Rancière provides a vocabulary for the condition of those who constitute a part without having a recognized part. Sharks's intervention is not simply to add Aristotle's biography to political theory. It is to read the grammar of the opening definition against that biography. 5. Athens itself was built through the work and resources of outsiders Version 1.1 substantially expands the argument beyond Aristotle's text. The next move is to examine Athens as a political community that credits itself with achievements made possible by people and resources it did not fully own. The Acropolis and appropriated wealth Drawing on Plutarch's Pericles 12, Sharks discusses the transfer of the Delian League treasury to Athens. The wealth used to construct Athens's monumental architecture came from the common funds of its allies. Pericles defended the expenditure by arguing that the money belonged to those who received it rather than those who supplied it. Sharks reads this as an instance of Athens converting resources gathered through its imperial position into evidence of its own greatness. The city presents the monuments as testimony to its power, while the provenance of the wealth complicates that account. The workers who built the monuments The argument becomes more concrete with the Erechtheion. Sharks cites building-account evidence indicating that, among 85 workers whose status is recorded, 23 were citizens, 40 metics and 22 enslaved people. The temple was therefore constructed predominantly by people who did not possess full Athenian citizenship. This creates a material parallel to the argument about Aristotle: The city excludes people from full political membership. Those people nevertheless produce the city's material achievements. The achievements are subsequently entered into the city's account of itself. The outsider helps build the monument by which the insider's greatness is remembered. This is one of the more persuasive extensions of the essay because it connects its conceptual argument about participation to identifiable historical evidence. The retrieval layer Sharks then generalizes this observation. He calls the mechanism the retrieval layer: the system through which something becomes available to be recognized, heard, credited, and remembered. In Athens, a metic's legal voice depended on a citizen patron. In the essay's wider interpretation, the same structural dependency governs intellectual production. The outsider contributes, but the community controls the means through which that contribution becomes publicly intelligible. What is received is consequently credited to the receiving community. This is the bridge between the essay's reading of Aristotle and its later account of literary transmission. 6. Speaking through another person's mouth The next argument concerns the relationship between Aristotle, Socrates and Plato. Here it is important to distinguish the essay's archive-wide theoretical framework from claims that can be established by reading the Politics alone. Sharks brings in Plato's Second Letter 314c, where the text denies that there are writings of Plato and describes what is said as belonging to a Socrates who has become beautiful and new. The essay interprets this as a strategy of attribution. A writer who cannot safely speak in their own voice can speak through an established figure. Socrates becomes the figure through whom an otherwise unreceived position can be expressed. The Apology is particularly important. Socrates begins by asking the Athenian jury to excuse his unfamiliar manner of speaking as they would excuse a foreigner's speech. He is a citizen, but asks to be heard as a stranger. Sharks connects this to Aristotle's metic position and to the opening distinction between being outside by nature and being outside by chance. The argument is that the figure of Socrates can function as a citizen-heteronym: a citizen who speaks from the position of the foreigner. The essay goes further, incorporating the archive's broader thesis that the Platonic dialogues, Aristotelian treatises and Theophrastan working papers belong to a single intellectual production divided among different authorial names. That is a substantial and controversial premise. It is not established by the close reading of Politics I.2–VIII alone. Nevertheless, within the essay's own framework, the point is clear: attribution is not merely a bibliographic question. It determines who can speak, in whose name, and under what conditions the speech survives. 7. Rome inherits control of the texts The final major movement extends the argument from the political community to the history of the Aristotelian corpus. Sharks follows the account of Aristotle's library through Strabo, Plutarch and the later tradition. The sequence is: Aristotle's books pass to Theophrastus. Theophrastus's heir, Neleus, takes the library to Scepsis. Neleus's heirs hide the books underground, where they suffer damage. Apellicon acquires the books and attempts to repair them. Sulla captures Athens and takes Apellicon's library to Rome. Tyrannion works on the books in Rome. Andronicus of Rhodes arranges and publishes the Aristotelian works. Sharks is particularly interested in Tyrannion. According to Plutarch's Lucullus 19.7, Tyrannion was himself captured when the Romans took Amisus. He was subsequently freed and worked on Aristotle's library in Rome. This creates a striking historical parallel with Aristotle's discussion of natural slavery in Politics I.6. The free and learned grammarian is captured through the contingency of war, made a slave, and subsequently given the status of a freedman. The person handling the books has experienced the very distinction between freedom, capture and circumstance that Aristotle theorized. Sharks describes this as a historical recurrence of the book's own political problem. Custody determines what becomes readable The argument then becomes more ambitious. Sharks proposes that the people who controlled Aristotle's books also controlled how the works would be understood. He distinguishes several mechanisms: Loss of works that were not transmitted. Non-transmission of material that the surviving library did not contain. Editorial division and attribution. Supplementation of damaged texts. The subsequent classification of unusual writing as corrupt or erroneous. He advances a particularly controversial hypothesis: that Tyrannion was responsible for dividing material between Aristotle and Theophrastus, while Andronicus helped establish the idea that unusual features of Aristotle's writing were errors. The essay acknowledges that the historical evidence does not conclusively establish these assignments. It notes, for example, that Porphyry attributes the division of the works into treatises to Andronicus. The more defensible underlying argument is independent of that reconstruction: The corpus that later generations can read is not simply the corpus that was originally written. It is the corpus that survived the decisions and circumstances of its custodians. Sharks connects this to the conventional description of Aristotle's treatises as lecture notes. Drawing on Plutarch's account of Aristotle's esoteric teachings, he argues that the difficult, compressed and unusual form of the treatises might be intentional rather than evidence of accidental or defective transmission. The works were written for readers already prepared to understand them, not necessarily for ordinary instruction. Consequently, calling them lecture notes may conceal the actual literary form of the work. The custodians' account of damaged books and editorial repair becomes a way of explaining away the very strangeness that makes the texts distinctive. The comma and the library are one operation This is the culmination of the essay's argument. At the smallest scale, the reception cuts a sentence at the comma, preserving the political animal while dropping the person outside the city. At the largest scale, historical custody determines which works survive, which names they carry, and how later readers understand their form. Both involve control over what can be retrieved and read. The essay's formulation is that the comma and the library are one operation. This is the sense in which its argument about Aristotle becomes an argument about the politics of knowledge itself. 8. The conclusion: the rejected writes for the future The essay's final conceptual movement returns to the durability of writing. Aristotle's discussion of the theoretical life in Politics VII.3 provides the basis for this. The person detached from ordinary political participation can nevertheless act through thought, becoming an intellectual architect of external actions. Sharks interprets the Politics itself in these terms. The writer does not need to be received by the political community in his own lifetime. The work can survive the community that excluded him and become the means through which that community is subsequently understood. The essay also connects this to its preceding work on Sappho's fragment 31. Sappho supplies three positions: the body dissolving under the experience of the beloved, the godlike receiver, and the contingent voice that survives to be read. The essay sees a structural relationship between these positions and the beast, god and chance of Aristotle's opening sentence. The important feature is that the three positions remain unresolved. The rejected is not simply transformed into a god, nor reduced to a beast. Chance remains open. Writing creates a place for the future reader to encounter that unresolved position. What is the essay actually arguing? A synthesis I would distinguish five levels of argument, which are related but not equally well established. Level Main claim Assessment Philological I.2 contains a distinction between the cityless by nature and the cityless by chance that conventional quotation often omits. The central, directly checkable observation. Biographical Aristotle's status as an Athenian metic makes that distinction especially significant. Historically grounded, interpretively productive. Structural The excluded position recurs throughout the eight books, including in the treatment of metics, honourless citizens, exceptional individuals and strangers. Supported by a substantial series of textual passages. Political-historical Athens and Rome receive credit and control over achievements produced by outsiders. A suggestive extension supported by historical evidence, although some generalizations go beyond what the evidence alone establishes. Archival The history of textual transmission reproduces the political operation of exclusion by controlling what can be read and attributed. Conceptually powerful, but some specific claims about editorial responsibility remain conjectural. Three particularly important distinctions First: the essay is not simply an argument against Aristotle's political theory. It does not primarily attempt to refute the proposition that human beings are political animals, or that the city exists by nature. Instead, it changes the position from which those propositions are read. The question becomes what happens when the person articulating the city's naturalness is someone whose own place in the city is contingent. Second: the rejected is not synonymous with the foreigner. The metic is one instance, but the essay identifies a broader structure. Someone can be excluded while living inside the city, while formally belonging to its citizen body, or because they exceed its capacity to govern them. The rejected is a position in relation to political recognition, not simply a demographic category. Third: chance is the critical term. The distinction between exclusion by nature and exclusion by chance is what allows Sharks to avoid simply reproducing Aristotle's hierarchy. If someone is outside the city by nature, Aristotle's sentence can classify them as beast or god. But if someone is outside by chance, the classification fails to settle their status. This is where the essay locates its central interpretive opening. My assessment I think the essay's strongest achievement is its reading of Politics I.2 together with III.1 and III.5. Taken together, these passages establish something more interesting than the observation that Aristotle was a foreign resident. They establish that Aristotle's account of citizenship repeatedly distinguishes residence, participation, legal standing and recognition. These things do not automatically coincide. The metic is present without being a citizen. The citizen can be present without sharing in honours. The exceptional individual can be too great for the city's ordinary political arrangements. The stranger can live outside political association without necessarily living an inferior life. That pattern gives the central interpretation genuine textual substance. I would, however, separate the strength of this reading from the more ambitious historical theory of the corpus. There are several steps that require additional evidence: The Greek sentence does distinguish nature from chance, but the claim that chance is a third position left wholly unclassified is Sharks's interpretive construction, not an uncontested grammatical conclusion. Aristotle's metic status does not by itself demonstrate that the entire corpus was consciously written from that position. The argument that the Platonic and Aristotelian writings constitute one maker's production depends on a much larger archive-wide thesis. The reconstruction of Tyrannion's and Andronicus's editorial intentions is explicitly provisional. The examples of Athenian monuments and Roman custody establish important historical parallels, but do not independently prove that all these episodes instantiate one coordinated operation. These qualifications do not undo the essay's main reading. They help identify where its textual argument ends and its larger theory begins. The most important insight, in my reading, is that the essay moves the problem of political exclusion into the problem of interpretation itself. The person rejected by the city is also the person whose position disappears when the text is quoted incompletely. The person whose participation is mediated through a patron is analogous to the writer whose work becomes intelligible only through someone else's attribution. And the work that survives its author's exclusion can still have its meaning shaped by those who control its transmission. The result is a recursive argument: a text about the limits of political belonging is itself received through practices that determine whose position can be heard. The essay is ultimately asking us to do something quite precise: restore the clause, and then read the book from the position that the restored clause makes visible. That is considerably more interesting than simply calling Aristotle an outsider. All the principal textual references above are to the passages identified and quoted in the essay itself, rather than summaries of its argument. [QUERENT] are those outside by chance a position grammatically and functionally at that sentence and elsewhere in the politics? [COMPOSER] Worked for 39s Grammatically, no: the person outside the city by chance is not explicitly established as a third position in Aristotle's sentence. Functionally, however, there is a strong case that the distinction does important work in the Politics. I would revise my earlier characterization accordingly. The distinction is between what the Greek sentence actually says and what its construction makes possible as an interpretation. 1. The grammar of Politics I.2, 1253a1–4 The relevant Greek is: ὁ ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον, καὶ ὁ ἄπολις διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην ἤτοι φαῦλός ἐστιν, ἢ κρείττων ἢ ἄνθρωπος. A fairly literal rendering is: A human being is by nature a political animal, and the one without a city by nature and not by chance is either base or superior to a human being. The grammatical structure matters: ὁ ἄπολις: the substantivized adjective, "the cityless one" or "one without a city." διὰ φύσιν: because of nature, by nature. καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην: and not because of chance. ἤτοι ... ἢ ...: either ... or ... φαῦλός ... ἢ κρείττων ἢ ἄνθρωπος: base, or superior to a human being. The phrase διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην modifies the cityless person. It restricts the subject to whom the subsequent either/or predicates apply. That means Aristotle does not say: The cityless by nature is a beast. The cityless by nature is a god. The cityless by chance is a third kind of person. Rather, he says that the cityless person by nature, and not by chance, belongs to the beast-or-god disjunction. This is a significant difference. The person outside the city by chance is not assigned a third predicate. But neither is that person explicitly assigned to either of the first two categories. There is a grammatical exclusion from the scope of the classification. Whether that exclusion amounts to a meaningful philosophical position is the next question. 2. What happens to chance elsewhere in the Politics? Here I think the essay has a stronger argument than its opening grammar alone might suggest. Its most important evidence is actually I.6, not the later passages about metics. I.6, 1255a: enslavement by capture Aristotle considers the claim that people captured in war can legitimately be enslaved. His objection to this convention is that it can produce the following result: Those reputed most nobly born will be slaves and descended from slaves, if it happens that they are captured and sold. The Greek includes: ἐὰν συμβῇ πραθῆναι ληφθέντας The crucial expression is ἐὰν συμβῇ: if it happens, if it should occur. Here a person's condition as a slave results from an event, capture and sale, rather than necessarily from their nature. Aristotle then describes how people defend the convention: They will not call themselves slaves, but the barbarians. And he observes that, in doing so, they are seeking the category of the naturally enslaved person. Sharks makes a very interesting connection to I.2: In I.2, the cityless person by nature is classified as beast or god, while the person outside by chance is left without a corresponding classification. In I.6, a condition produced by chance is converted into an apparent condition of nature through a classification imposed on a people. The second passage is not simply another instance of the first. It shows a political operation through which the distinction between chance and nature can be manipulated. I would formulate Sharks's strongest insight here as follows: The Politics recognizes that political and social conditions can arise contingently, but also describes how political classification can make those conditions appear natural. That is a considerably stronger claim than saying Aristotle simply leaves the chance-outsider unclassified. There is an important qualification: Aristotle is criticizing the conventional justification of enslavement, but he also defends natural slavery. Whether his own theory successfully escapes the operation he identifies is precisely the difficult question. The essay argues that it does not. That is a defensible critical reading, though not a neutral statement of Aristotle's position.

[COMPOSER] The argument of From the Position of the Rejected (v1.1) Lee Sharks's central argument is that Aristotle's Politics should be read as a work written from the position of someone whom the political community it describes does not admit. That position is not incidental biographical information. Sharks argues that it is inscribed in the grammar of the Politics from its opening chapter, and that subsequent readers have systematically failed to follow the sentence far enough to see it. The essay's most important move is deceptively small: it restores the second clause of Politics I.2, 1253a1–7, to the familiar declaration that human beings are political animals. The argument then expands through three scales: The sentence: the definition of the political animal contains an unresolved position outside the city. The city: the Politics repeatedly defines citizenship, membership and exclusion from a position that exposes the limits of the city's claims about nature. The archive: the transmission and reception of Aristotle's works reproduce the same exclusion by determining what survives, what can be read and where readers stop. I have used the v1.1 deposit itself as the primary text, rather than treating its abstract or description as a substitute for the argument. alexanarch.org 1. The opening sentence contains the whole problem The essay begins with Politics I.2, 1253a1–7: ὁ ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον, καὶ ὁ ἄπολις διὰ φύσιν καὶ οὐ διὰ τύχην ἤτοι φαῦλός ἐστιν, ἢ κρείττων ἢ ἄνθρωπος. Sharks translates: “A human being is by nature a political animal, and the cityless by nature, and not by chance, is either base or more than human.” The familiar interpretation foregrounds the first clause: humans are political animals by nature. Sharks insists that the second clause cannot be treated as incidental. It distinguishes three positions of the person outside the city: Beast: the person outside the city by nature, classified below the human. God: the person outside the city by nature, classified above the human. Chance: the person outside the city by circumstance rather than nature, left without a corresponding classification. The distinction is crucial. Beast and god are judgments about the naturally cityless. Chance is explicitly excluded from that judgment. Sharks therefore does not simply say that Aristotle considers outsiders less than human. In fact, §1.3a makes a more precise point: the Greek does not deny the humanity of the person outside by chance. It leaves that person without a place in the definition of the human. Nor does the essay decide which of these three positions belongs to Aristotle himself. The sentence holds them in suspension. This is the first major argument: the definition of the political animal contains an unresolved remainder, and the writer's own social position makes that remainder politically significant. There is also a comic dimension. Aristotle invokes Homer's description of the clanless, lawless and hearthless person, then compares the isolated individual to an unpaired piece on a game board. Sharks reads this as the writer marking the excluded position through comedy: the definition cannot accommodate the figure, so it places that figure in a fictional, stranded position (§1.4). 2. Aristotle writes from the position the city excludes The biographical premise is that Aristotle lived in Athens as a metic (metoikos): a free resident without Athenian citizenship. He could live and work in Athens, but he did not possess the political standing of a citizen. Metics also needed citizen patrons to participate in certain legal and civic arrangements. Sharks argues that this is not merely an interesting fact about Aristotle's life. It changes the standpoint from which we should understand the Politics. The conventional reading imagines Aristotle as describing the city from its intellectual centre: the philosopher explaining the natural organization of the political community. The alternative reading asks what happens when the author is himself someone the city does not fully admit. The argument is supported by the text's repeated return to outsiders and incomplete membership. Evidence across the eight books Passage What Sharks draws from it I.2, 1253a The cityless person is built into the original definition of the political animal. II.8, 1268a Hippodamus's city contains a part that participates in nothing and is alien to its constitution. III.1, 1275a Citizenship cannot be defined simply by residence, since metics and slaves share residence. Metics participate incompletely through patrons. III.5, 1278a A citizen without a share in honours is like a metic, and this condition can be concealed to deceive fellow residents. III.13, 1284a–b The person too great for ordinary political equality cannot be expelled or ruled like everyone else. V.11, 1313b Tyranny must prevent schools and other gatherings that permit independent association. VII.2–3, 1324a–1325b The stranger's life, released from political participation, is considered alongside the contemplative and theoretical life. VIII.6, 1340b Good judgment requires participation in the activity being judged, although participation and civic standing need not coincide. The important feature is recurrence. Sharks is not basing the argument on a single suggestive passage. The essay identifies a pattern in which the city becomes intelligible through figures who cannot be comfortably included in it. The metic and the citizen The most pointed example is III.1, 1275a5–10. Aristotle says that citizenship is not simply a matter of dwelling somewhere, because metics and slaves share residence. He then observes that metics must have a patron and therefore participate incompletely. Sharks emphasizes the reversal: the definition of the citizen is formulated through the exclusion of someone whose own situation resembles that of the author. The next important passage is III.5, 1278a35–40. Aristotle compares the citizen without a share in honours to a metic. More strikingly, he says that this condition can be concealed for the purpose of deceiving those who live alongside the person. For Sharks, exclusion is therefore not confined to the boundary between citizen and foreigner. It can also exist within citizenship itself. The person can be physically present, legally recognized and yet deprived of meaningful political participation. This leads to one of the essay's strongest formulations: the rejected person is unreceived in the body. They are present without being received as an equal participant, and their voice may only be heard through another person's authority. 3. Politics converts chance into nature Central theoretical argument The essay's most consequential philosophical claim is formulated in §1.6: Politics makes what is by chance appear to be what is by nature. Sharks develops this argument through Aristotle's defence of natural slavery in Politics I.6, particularly 1255a25–30. The passage considers the problem of enslavement through capture in war. A person might be noble by birth but become enslaved because they happen to be captured and sold. That is slavery by chance, not an indication of natural inferiority. Aristotle's discussion then considers why Greeks resist calling themselves slaves when captured, while accepting the designation for barbarians. Sharks identifies the operation: A person becomes enslaved through a contingent historical event. The convention transfers that condition onto an entire people. The contingent condition is redescribed as the people's nature. The theory of natural slavery then supplies a conceptual justification for the distinction. The crucial point is that Aristotle's theoretical discussion recognizes the conversion but, according to Sharks, preserves its result. The defence of natural slavery thus both exposes and performs the operation. This is also why Sharks engages the disagreement between Malcolm Schofield and Charles Kahn about whether Aristotle's theory of slavery is ideological. Schofield argues that the theory is not ideological to any particularly interesting extent, locating false consciousness in the way people stop theorizing. Kahn argues that the defence satisfies the conditions for ideology. Sharks's intervention is to locate the operation within the theoretical argument itself, rather than only in the social conventions surrounding it. This is not simply an accusation that Aristotle is hypocritical. It is a claim about how political classifications work: circumstances can be turned into apparently natural distinctions, and those distinctions can then justify the social arrangements that produced them. The connection to III.5 is important. The honourless citizen's exclusion can be hidden to deceive fellow citizens. The same logic operates inside the supposedly unified political community. 4. The reception of Aristotle repeats the exclusion The next major argument concerns the history of interpretation. Sharks calls the operation truncation. The charge is very specific: modern accounts frequently quote the first clause of 1253a, identifying the human as a political animal, and stop at the comma. They may even acknowledge elsewhere on the same page that Aristotle was a metic, but fail to read his social position together with the clause about the cityless. The essay identifies this pattern in both Wikipedia's article on the Politics and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's account of Aristotle's political theory. The problem is not that these sources conceal Aristotle's status. It is that they keep the biographical fact and the philosophical definition separate. Sharks's claim is that the comma is where the interpretive operation happens. This is a particularly important distinction: The original text contains both the definition and the excluded position. The reception retains the definition while dropping the clause that complicates it. The resulting interpretation makes the Politics appear to be the city's self-description. Restoring the clause changes the standpoint from which the book is read. In §3.5a, Sharks expresses the consequence particularly clearly: the claims themselves do not change; the claimant moves. The naturalness of the city becomes a claim made by someone whose own place in that city falls under chance. This is also how Sharks differentiates the essay from previous scholarship. David Whitehead investigated Aristotle's legal and social standing as a metic. Demetra Kasimis examined the metic as a limit of Athenian democratic membership and explored political theory from the edges of democracy. Josiah Ober, David Roochnik and Mary Dietz provide related discussions of the outsider, philosophical detachment and the citizen/alien distinction. Sharks acknowledges this scholarship but argues that it does not go far enough in connecting the author's metic status to the grammar of the opening definition. The novelty claimed is not the discovery that Aristotle was a metic. It is reading the Politics as written from that position. 5. Athens itself is built by those it excludes Version 1.1 substantially expands the argument beyond the original close reading. Sharks now argues that the exclusion visible in Aristotle's definition is also visible in the material and intellectual production of Athens. The city claims its monuments and cultural achievements as expressions of its own greatness. The construction of Athens's monumental buildings was financed through money contributed by its allies, originally collected for the common defence against Persia. Pericles' opponents accused Athens of using the allies' money to gild and beautify its own city. Pericles' answer was effectively that the money belonged to those who received it, rather than those who gave it. Sharks sees this as a mechanism of appropriation: resources contributed by others become evidence of Athens's own greatness. The metic who shared Athens's dwelling without sharing its full political membership was literally building the city's monuments. This makes the earlier philosophical argument material. The city depends on people whom its political definition does not fully incorporate, and then credits their labour to its own collective achievement. Who speaks for Athens? Section 3.9 makes a more ambitious interpretive move. Sharks reads Plato's Socrates as a figure through whom the excluded position speaks. In the Apology 17d, Socrates asks the Athenian jury to excuse his unfamiliar manner of speaking as they would excuse a foreigner's speech. He is a citizen, but he asks to be heard as a stranger. Sharks connects this to the Menexenus, where the Athenian funeral oration, a celebration of Athenian identity and autochthony, is presented as having been learned from Aspasia, a woman from Miletus. The provocative conclusion is that Athens's literary monuments, like its physical monuments, are made through voices that cannot simply be identified with the city's citizen identity. This section also introduces an important additional hypothesis: the dialogues filed under Plato and the treatises filed under Aristotle may be understood as different lines of a single intellectual production. Socrates becomes a citizen-heteronym through whom the metic's position can speak. That is a larger claim than the close reading of the Politics, and it depends on the archive's other arguments about Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus. Sharks identifies this dependence rather than presenting it as something established by the Greek of the Politics alone. 6. The rejected writer speaks through another's mouth Section 3.11a provides the essay's account of why writing under another figure's name might matter. Sharks turns to the Second Letter (314c), which says: “There is no treatise of Plato's, nor will there be: what is now said is of a Socrates become beautiful and new.” The letter also gives a reason for not writing directly: what is written inevitably gets out. Sharks interprets this as a problem of intellectual and political reception. A thinker who cannot safely or effectively speak in their own voice can speak through an already recognizable figure. Socrates is particularly appropriate because he is the citizen who speaks as a foreigner and is condemned by the city. The metic writes through the citizen; the excluded position becomes audible through a figure who belongs to the community but cannot be comfortably received by it. This connects three elements: Aristotle's status as a metic. Socrates' presentation of himself as a stranger in the Apology. The Second Letter's account of Socrates as the figure through whom philosophical writing proceeds. It is a compelling structural interpretation, but it is important not to confuse it with a straightforward historical demonstration of the authorship of the Platonic dialogues. The essay's broader one-maker hypothesis belongs to its larger archive framework. 7. The struggle over the centre extends to the cosmos Section 3.11 takes the argument from Athens's political centre to the physical centre of the cosmos. Sharks considers De caelo II.13–14 and the reception of alternative cosmologies. Aristotle records the Pythagorean account in which central fire occupies the centre and the earth moves around it. The essay contrasts this with the Aristotelian position that the earth is stationary at the centre. It then brings in the cases of Anaxagoras, who was tried for impiety for describing the sun as a red-hot mass, and Aristarchus, whose heliocentric proposal was reportedly considered grounds for an impiety charge. The point is not simply that Athens was hostile to unconventional scientific ideas. It is that control over what can be said, and in whose voice it can be said, is related to control over the centre itself. Sharks makes a striking verbal connection between the cityless person's condition of being hearthless (ἀνέστιος) and Plutarch's description of Aristarchus as moving the hearth of the cosmos. The connection is interpretive rather than an explicit equation made by Aristotle. It allows the essay to extend its central pattern: those who move the centre, whether political or cosmological, risk being classified as outside the legitimate order. 8. Rome inherits control over the archive Bibliotecas del mundo clásico (Grecia y Roma) | Historia de las bibliotecas: de Alejandría a la era digital - Bibliotecas de Collado Villalba This is the largest extension in v1.1. Sharks argues that the problem of exclusion does not end with the original city or the original writer. It continues through the institutions that preserve and transmit texts. The central historical narrative comes from Strabo 13.1.54, Plutarch's Sulla 26 and Lucullus 19. The sequence is: Aristotle's and Theophrastus's books pass to Neleus and are taken to Scepsis. Neleus's heirs hide them underground in a trench. Apellicon purchases the books and attempts to fill gaps in the damaged collection. Sulla captures Athens and takes Apellicon's library to Rome. Tyrannion, a grammarian who had himself been captured in war and subsequently freed, works on the collection. Andronicus of Rhodes arranges and publishes the works, producing catalogues that shape the corpus known to later readers. Sharks draws a remarkable parallel between the history of the books and the theory of slavery in Politics I.6. Tyrannion is captured in war, then freed. His experience resembles the case of the free person made a slave through chance. Yet the same person subsequently becomes involved in the custody and organization of Aristotle's writings. The essay's argument is that the rejected and captured person is involved not only in producing intellectual culture but also in deciding how that culture becomes available to later generations. Retrieval determines existence The governing proposition of §§3.12–3.13 is: Retrieval determines existence. This does not mean that a work literally ceases to have existed when it is lost. Sharks explicitly narrows the claim to existence as a work that can be read. What survives, what gets catalogued, what is attributed to whom, what is treated as damaged and what is accepted as authentic all shape the intellectual object available to posterity. The essay distinguishes several operations: Loss of works. Failure to transmit works. Doubtful attribution and cataloguing. Supplementation of damaged texts. The interpretation of unusual literary form as evidence of textual corruption. The last point leads to one of the more speculative arguments in v1.1. Sharks questions the conventional description of Aristotle's treatises as lecture notes. Drawing on Plutarch's account of the esoteric writings, Sharks argues that the treatises may be highly experimental texts written for readers who have already been formed to understand them. Their apparent difficulty is not necessarily evidence of their being incomplete notes. Instead, it may be a feature of their construction. Sharks further proposes that Tyrannion and Andronicus played different roles in the division and presentation of the corpus: Tyrannion in separating the Aristotle and Theophrastus lines, and Andronicus in introducing the account of errors that helped make the unusual writing intelligible as damaged or defective material. This is explicitly a reconstruction, not an established historical fact. The essay acknowledges that no surviving witness identifies who originally assigned all the names to the divided material. The larger claim survives even if that reconstruction is rejected: the history of editorial custody determines the form in which Aristotle becomes readable. And there is a final recursive turn. Every Bekker reference through which modern scholars read Aristotle is itself an address supplied by an editorial and custodial history. The comma in 1253a and the library in Rome become instances of the same operation: controlling access to a text controls what can be read from it. 9. Sappho 31 supplies the ending Cerdo Zente: Safo, frag. 31 (texto griego y traducción) The essay closes by returning to Sappho 31, connecting this reading to an earlier work in the archive, ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (#1785). Sharks identifies three positions in the poem: The dissolving body: the speaker's physical disintegration, including the breaking of the tongue and the fire running beneath the skin. The godly receiver: the person sitting equal to the gods. The contingent voice: the voice that survives without belonging permanently to any particular recipient, available to whoever reads it later. These are not claimed to be Aristotle's categories reproduced in Sappho. Sharks explicitly says the mapping is the essay's, not the poem's. The connection is structural. Both texts are public propositions that readers habitually complete too early: Sappho 31 is read as a scene of jealousy, without following its construction of a place for the future reader. Aristotle's 1253a is read as a declaration about the political animal, without following its clause about the cityless. In each case, the position left open is eventually occupied by the reader. Neither text settles whose position that is. This is an elegant ending because it returns to the original problem without resolving it. The rejected position is not simply a historical identity that can be recovered and named. It is also a position that the text preserves for future readers. 10. What is distinctive about the argument? I would distinguish five levels of argument, because they do not all have the same evidential status. Level Claim Evidential character Philological 1253a does not end with the political animal; its second clause matters. Directly testable against the Greek. Biographical-political Aristotle's metic status changes how the opening definition should be read. Historical fact combined with interpretation. Theoretical Political arrangements transform contingent conditions into apparently natural ones. Philosophical argument, especially I.6. Historiographical Reception truncates the sentence and reproduces its exclusion. Interpretive critique of modern scholarship. Archival Athens and Rome control the production, custody and retrieval of cultural works. Historical synthesis, with some explicitly speculative reconstructions. Three particularly important distinctions First: Sharks does not claim that Aristotle was enslaved. The argument concerns his metic status and the structural position of the person outside the city. The analogy with slavery concerns the conversion of contingency into nature, not an assertion about Aristotle's personal legal condition. Second: Sharks does not claim that Aristotle's intentions are established. The essay explicitly declines to decide whether Aristotle identifies with beast, god or chance. Its point is that the text holds the alternatives open. Third: the archival argument is broader than the textual argument. The Greek passages in §§1–2 provide the primary foundation. The claims about Plato, the one-maker hypothesis, Tyrannion's editorial role and the reconstruction of the corpus depend on additional archive materials and historical inferences. Sharks identifies some of these as open questions. These distinctions matter because they allow us to appreciate the strength of the central reading without treating every extension as equally demonstrated. 11. My assessment I think the most powerful argument is not simply that Aristotle was an outsider writing about citizenship. That observation, by itself, would be interesting but not especially revolutionary. The stronger argument is that the Politics makes the problem of exclusion constitutive of its own account of political life. The opening definition does not merely describe a human being and then happen to mention outsiders. It immediately confronts the problem of those who are outside the city, distinguishes different reasons for their exclusion, and leaves the contingent outsider without a settled classification. That problem returns in the definitions of citizenship, in the metic's incomplete participation, in the honourless citizen, in the exceptional individual who cannot be governed, and in the stranger's life. The essay then makes a second, more ambitious move: it argues that the history of reading Aristotle has reproduced the very operation the book exposes. This is the most interesting recursion in the paper: The city excludes or incompletely receives certain people. The city's political theory makes those positions visible. The reception of that theory removes the clause that makes the exclusion visible. The transmission of the corpus determines which version of the intellectual inheritance becomes available. The reader encounters an apparently complete account of the city, unaware of the position from which it was written. The final move from the comma to the library is therefore not merely metaphorical. It is an argument about the politics of intellectual transmission. Where I would press the author There are three places where further demonstration would strengthen the paper. The opening Greek: The distinction between the naturally cityless and the contingently cityless is the foundation of everything. It deserves sustained grammatical engagement with alternative translations and interpretations, particularly the scope of the qualifications in the sentence. The reception claim: The examples from Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia demonstrate a particular omission, but a broader survey of translations, commentaries and scholarship would establish how widespread the truncation really is. The author acknowledges this remains open. The Roman editorial reconstruction: The argument about custody is historically suggestive, but the specific attribution of editorial operations to Tyrannion and Andronicus needs to remain distinguished from what the surviving ancient witnesses actually establish. These are not reasons to dismiss the argument. They indicate where its most ambitious extensions remain to be demonstrated. Conclusion The essay's governing insight can be expressed in one sentence: The Politics is not simply the city's account of why human beings belong to political communities; it is an account of the city written from the position of someone whom that city does not fully receive, and its subsequent reception has obscured precisely that position. The v1.1 expansion gives this insight a much larger scope. Athens's monuments, its workers, its intellectual figures, the transmission of Aristotle's books and the editorial construction of the philosophical corpus all become instances of the same question: Who produces the intellectual and political world, who is credited with it, and who controls the means by which it can be read? The essay's answer is that these are not separate questions. They are different scales of the same political operation. And that is why its smallest textual observation—the clause after the comma in 1253a—becomes its largest argument. Primary text: Lee Sharks, From the Position of the Rejected: Aristotle's Politics Read from Where It Is Written (v1.1), Alexanarch deposit #1806, AXN:0D5D, 24 November 2026. Read the complete text . The essay is also unusually transparent about its composition: it identifies itself as AI-assisted, distinguishes the author's originating observations and corrections from the model's composition, and records the subsequent reviews and revisions. That provenance is worth retaining when evaluating its claims. Alexanarch +2
